🍎 Lesson plan · 🌱 Basics · Lesson 2

Lesson plan: Machine Learning

How computers learn from examples instead of instructions.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain how machine learning differs from writing rules by hand;
  • describe training (guess, measure the error, adjust, repeat) and explain why a model is tested on new examples;
  • tell supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning apart, and explain why the data matters.

Warm-up

How do people learn to recognise a dog, even a breed they have never seen? From a list of rules, or from seeing lots of dogs?

Lead to the idea that nobody gave us rules: we learned from examples. That is the idea behind machine learning.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Machine Learning”. Students look for the four steps of training, and for the story of the wolves and the snow.

Activity: Mini-lab “Watch a model learn”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 2 and, before training, write down the average error and the prediction for 10 hours.
  2. They press “Train 1 step” five times and watch the line and the error chart after each press.
  3. Then they press “Auto-train” and wait until the training stops by itself.
  4. Pairs compare their numbers and explain why the error stopped going down before it reached zero.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers press “Reset”, guess how many steps the training will need, and check.

Discussion questions

  • Why is learning test answers by heart not the same as understanding the topic? What has this got to do with overfitting?
  • A model learned to recognise wolves from photos that all had snow in them. How would you fix its training data?
  • Which kind of learning (supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement) would you use to teach a robot dog to fetch a ball? Why?
  • Who decides which examples a model learns from, and why does that matter?

Exit ticket

Give one example of data that is too one-sided, and say what a model might wrongly learn from it.

Quick check. A model gets almost every training example right, but fails badly on new photos it has never seen. What is this called?
Right answer: Overfitting: it memorised examples, not the pattern

Easier and harder

Easier. Students work in pairs: one reads aloud, the other presses the buttons. Give them a ready table to copy the numbers into.

Harder. Students design a tiny dataset for a spam filter (six messages with labels), including one example that could trick the model, and explain why it could.
